shravanvinayhegde / predictive-maintenance-pytorch

Remaining Useful Life,
read straight off the sensors.

Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction for aircraft turbofan engines, built entirely on PyTorch, benchmarked on NASA's C-MAPSS engine degradation dataset. This site is a code-grounded review of the implementation — not a tutorial — for engineers auditing architecture, data handling, and evaluation methodology.

Open project map → View NASA_pytorch.ipynb
02

Data pipeline

Download → EDA → RUL labeling → engine-grouped split → standardization → sliding windows → Dataset/DataLoader. Nine stages, each traced to its notebook cell.

 03

Model architecture

MLP, 1D-CNN, LSTM, GRU — four PyTorch models sharing one input/output contract, plus a Random Forest used strictly as a benchmark. Layer-by-layer tensor shapes.

 04

Training & evaluation

One shared training loop for all four networks — Adam, MSE loss, per-epoch validation MAE — plus the held-out test scoring function.

 05

Results

MAE / RMSE / R² across all five models on NASA's official test engines, plus documented limitations and extension paths.

Core hyperparameters

seed 42
WINDOW_SIZE 30 cycles Sequence length fed to every model
RUL_CAP 125 cycles Piecewise-linear RUL target cap
BATCH_SIZE 64 DataLoader batching
EPOCHS 10 Training loop
LR 1e-3 Adam optimizer learning rate
Train/val split 80% / 20%, grouped by engine GroupShuffleSplit(test_size=0.2)
Random seed 42 torch.manual_seed, np.random.seed, random_state

Scope of this documentation

NASA_pytorch.ipynb is the only notebook this site documents in depth — it's the repository's core predictive-maintenance deliverable. Experiments/ and Quick-Reaps/ hold separate, unrelated PyTorch notebooks (image/audio/text classification, and PyTorch fundamentals references) kept in the same repository for convenience; see the repository page for what each one covers.
